planting.note: Set small divisions or rooted cuttings into a sharply drained scree or alpine trough mix in spring; disturb roots as little as possible, since this cushion plant resents transplanting and establishes extremely slowly.

directions: Diapensia forms a dense, woody-based cushion of tiny leathery evergreen leaves studded in late spring with small white to blush-pink, five-petaled flowers, a hallmark of wind-scoured alpine fellfields on the highest summits of New England and the circumboreal arctic. It demands constant cold, intense light, and gritty, humus-poor, perfectly drained mineral soil; it cannot tolerate summer heat, humidity, or standing moisture and is essentially a specialist alpine-trough or scree-bed plant rather than a general garden subject. Growth is measured in millimeters per year, so patience is mandatory and any root disturbance can set a plant back for seasons. Best attempted only in cold, high-elevation or far-northern gardens with true alpine culture.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society (Native Plant Trust)

planting.note: Divide loose tufts in spring and transplant into constantly saturated, acidic sphagnum peat or bog-garden soil; grows naturally scattered through quaking sphagnum mats of cold northern bogs and fens rather than in dense stands.

directions: Boreal bog sedge is a slender, loosely tufted grasslike perennial of circumboreal sphagnum bogs and poor fens, sending up wiry stems topped with small, drooping, blackish-purple to dark brown spikelets in late spring to early summer. It is a true cold-bog specialist, needing permanently saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic peat and cool root conditions year-round, making it best suited to constructed bog gardens, peat-based container bogs, or naturalistic wetland restorations in cold climates. Combine with cottongrasses, sundews, and leatherleaf for an authentic northern peatland planting; it will not persist in fertile garden soil or where the peat is allowed to dry.

planting.note: Transplant divided rhizome sections in spring directly into floating peat mats or shallow standing water at a bog garden's margin; this sedge roots into saturated, unstable peat and often grows partly submerged.

directions: Mud sedge is a fine-leaved, bluish-green circumboreal sedge that roots directly into the floating sphagnum mats and shallow interstitial pools of cold, nutrient-poor bogs, often standing with its base submerged for much of the growing season. Slender stems carry small, dark, blackish spikelets in early summer above arching, grasslike foliage. It is a specialist for authentic peatland recreations and floating bog mats rather than conventional wet gardens, requiring permanently saturated, acidic, oxygen-poor peat and cool conditions; it is a good companion for pitcher plants, sundews, and cranberry on a constructed sphagnum raft or peat-lined bog pool. It does not tolerate fertilized soil, drying, or competition from vigorous wetland grasses.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container stock in spring directly into saturated, acidic peat; this low, non-suckering willow forms scattered individual clumps rather than thickets and pairs naturally with leatherleaf and sedges along a bog's edge.

directions: Bog willow is a low, smooth-barked shrub of circumboreal peatlands, bearing oval, bluish-green leaves with a pale, whitened underside and small, upright catkins that open before the leaves in spring. Unlike many willows it stays compact and does not form dense colonial thickets, instead growing as scattered individual shrubs rooted in the saturated, acidic peat of bogs and poor fens alongside sphagnum, leatherleaf, and bog sedges. It needs constantly wet, nutrient-poor, acidic soil and cool summer conditions, making it a good structural shrub for a constructed peat bog garden or restoration planting in cold climates, but it will decline in ordinary garden soil or warm, humid summers. Provide full sun and permanently saturated footing, and avoid disturbing its shallow root system once established.
